body.html:
Barkpark · self-update · from nag to product · W1–W6 shipped, epic closed

Self-update: from nag to product

Rev 3 — 2026-07-11. W1–W6 SHIPPED; epic closed. The instance self-update nag became an operator-facing product: a canary-gated fleet train, a fleet-wide kill switch, honest pinning, and real end-to-end rollback.

An admin opened Studio and saw an “Update available — Barkpark 0.2.24 (you run 0.0.83)” banner and said: “I always see this thing and can do nothing about it.” The banner was truthful — that box genuinely ran an April v0.0.83 build — but it was passive chrome: no button, no changelog, no dismiss. This paper is the record of turning instance self-update into a real product.

What already exists (do not rebuild)

• SelfUpdate.Checker — hourly upstream poll; caches :behind + a commit digest, and (W2) curated notes_body/notes_url. ON in prod.
• SelfUpdate.Runner — executes scripts/self-update.sh (git fast-forward → post-merge hook rebuild + restart) via a Port; bounded log; single-flight. Gated OFF unless BARKPARK_SELF_UPDATE_APPLY=1.
• SelfUpdateController — admin-only POST/GET /v1/admin/self-update (trigger + status + log tail + check).

The gap was never the engine — it was the surface and the automation.

Wave 1 — The Update-now bar (SHIPPED, PR #1195)

A slim strip pinned above the Studio topbar. Update now drives the existing executor and reports progress through the rebuild+restart, then reloads. What’s changed expands the digest as a changelog. × dismisses, persisted per-release in localStorage. Where apply is off it degrades to *How to update* guidance.

Design decision: the bar is layout chrome outside the LiveView diff, so it is driven by a vanilla delegated listener, not a phx-hook, and authenticates its fetch with the raw session token Studio already stamps into the DOM. The poller treats the mid-rebuild connection drop as expected and guards against a stale prior done triggering a false reload.

Wave 2 — Curated release notes (SHIPPED, PR #1197)

“What’s changed” was raw commit subjects. W2 makes a real changelog: the Checker fetches curated notes per vA.B.C (fetch_notes/3, checker.ex:164-169) and surfaces notes_body/notes_url on the :behind status; the Update bar’s What’s-changed links the notes when present and falls back to the commit digest otherwise. Notes are readable standalone (own URL) and covered by checker_test.exs.

Wave 3 — The release-curation agent (SHIPPED, PR #1199)

“Latest” used to mean “newest tag,” only as trustworthy as whoever tagged. W3 adds a curation agent: scripts/release-scan.sh reviews commits since the last release tag; .claude/workflows/release-curator.md judges whether a given HEAD is good (gates green, no pending reverts, no known-bad markers) with written rationale, drafts the W2 changelog, and proposes vA.B.C. “Latest” now means blessed, not merely new — under the bless policy below.

Wave 4 — Fleet autoupdate (SHIPPED, PR #1230)

“Update everyone.” The control plane (barkpark.cloud) rolls a blessed release across the fleet serially — cohort of 1: autoupdate_rollout_worker.ex advances one Registry.next_autoupdate_candidate/0 at a time (oldest-stale first), proving each instance live on the new release before touching the next. A 20-min settle gate re-reads each in-flight box’s own live verdict; a box that fails to settle is auto-pause_autoupdated so a bad box is contained, not retried. Growing cohorts stay a v2 optimisation.

Settled decisions (ratified 2026-07-10)

• Bless policy (W3): agent-proposes / human-publishes is the default — the curator drafts notes and proposes the tag, a human blesses the actual tag+publish. Fully autonomous tag-on-green is authorized only once the staging gate is live (W5 canary).
• Autoupdate default (W4): opt-OUT per tenant — autoupdate is on unless a tenant pauses or pins.
• Cohort size: cohort of 1 (serial) for v1 — the safest canary; growing cohorts deferred to v2.
• Per-instance control: pause / pin exist per instance (a failed settle auto-pauses); the affordance is real and surfaced honestly (W5 pin-honesty).

Wave 5 — from pipeline to product (SHIPPED, PR #2227)

Self-update stopped being a pipeline only insiders could see and became operator-facing product. #2227 landed five slices as one train:

1. Canary-gated fleet — a channel column (“prod” default, “staging”) on registry barkparks; AutoupdateRolloutWorker advances the staging box first and refuses to advance any prod box until a staging box is settled-current on the latest release. The gate fails OPEN when no staging box is registered, CLOSED once one exists.
2. Fleet-wide kill switch — a persisted autoupdate_halted flag in the CP DB, checked first by the worker every tick; operator-gated GET /v1/admin/autoupdate + POST …/halt / …/resume. The operator’s big red button, distinct from per-instance auto-pause.
3. Pin-honest trigger — a pinned instance refuses non-forced triggers with a 409 that NAMES the pin (error.pinned_release), so the console modal can say which release holds the box. The manual Update button no longer silently bypasses a pin.
4. Operator update panel — per-instance current/available version, channel, last-check, pin/pause state in the cloud console, with pin/pause/resume writes and the fleet halt switch. Honest loading / empty / error states.
5. CLI update truth + digest — bp cloud decodes full update+policy truth; bp cloud autoupdate pin|unpin|pause|resume + bp cloud rollout halt|resume|status; and a plain-text DailyDigestWorker mails the curator’s daily fleet verdict to platform admins.

Wave 6 — rollback becomes real (SHIPPED, PR #2514)

An operator staring at a bad release clicks Rollback in the console or runs bp cloud rollback <instance>. The instance resets its shared checkout to the idle slot’s recorded sha, reboots that slot, health-gates it on its own port, flips Caddy ONLY on green, rewrites deploy STATE, and the CP atomically pins the instance at the rolled-back version so the 5-minute rollout worker can never silently undo the operator. Every refusal is typed and honest. One path, zero new capabilities — the verb is a mode of the sanctioned deploy machinery riding the exact W5 relay seam.

• Flip+reset, never flip-only. A slot restart runs mix phx.server against the ONE shared checkout, so a bare port-flip recompiles whatever source is checked out (the mix-staleness probe caught it serving new code). git reset --hard <slot-sha> restores the old code byte-identically — the script’s own sanctioned failure-path idiom.
• Per-slot version stamp. Every deploy writes .slots/<target>.sha; rollback reads the idle slot’s stamp and refuses no_previous_slot (exit 21) when the stamp or a complete _build_<other>/prod is missing.
• Rollback lives in `instance-deploy.sh` as --rollback + --rollback-preflight, sharing the deploy flock. Typed exits: 21 no_previous_slot, 22 not_supported, 23 lock-held / already_running, 24 unhealthy_fail_closed. On unhealthy the slot is disabled, Caddy untouched, checkout reset back — fail closed.
• Instance API POST /v1/admin/rollback → 202 {status:“started”, target_sha} (same require_admin pipeline as self-update); sync preflight hands the CP the pin value, the async Port shares one run slot with self-update.
• CP relay POST /v1/barkparks/:id/rollback, gated require_primary_team_admin. Registry.trigger_rollback/2 does NOT block on pinned_release (rollback re-pins by design); on the instance 202 it atomically writes pinned_release = <instance-reported target> (never operator free-text) — pin-after-202 — then refreshes status. An unpinned rollback would be undone within one tick; a pinned one is immune with zero new worker logic.
• Console Rollback button in the W5 update panel, with typed conflict copy and schema-stays-forward wording: rolling back code does not undo a migration — write a compensating one.
• `bp cloud rollback <instance>` — raw-verbatim -o json, both refusal shapes decoded, a typed exit ladder (409→6, 404→4, 502→8, auth→3), and an honest STARTED-not-done verdict carrying the pin + the schema-forward law.

Where the epic closed — the honest remainders

The epic closed done with exactly two blessed open children — two live threads deliberately left burning, each a self-sufficient task carrying a recipe a stranger could execute:

• `isu-backlog-rollback-live-smoke` — the live smoke, PARKED as a recipe: a disposable box hand-minted from the warm image (Caddy tls internal, no real DNS via curl --resolve), TWO forward deploys to populate both slots, then rollback + deny cases. guerrilla is production AND the task ledger — never the first flip.
• `isu-backlog-operator-principal` — the kill-switch reachability bug: the fleet halt/resume routes are gated by require_worker (the faceless worker token), so neither a console session nor bp cloud rollout can reach them today (both degrade honestly). The deliberate next step is a platform-admin principal or a blessed worker-token-only posture — not two more surfaces inventing two more answers.

Deliberately unfiled (file only on demand): growing canary cohorts (the v2 per the rollout worker’s own moduledoc) and a maintenance-window gate for the rollout worker. Neither is debt; both are future options with no owner yet.
